title: Abstracts or full text? Evaluating input scope and computational efficiency in biomedical lay summarization
authors: Egecan Çelik Evgin, İlknur Karadeniz, Olcay Taner Yıldız
abstract: Biomedical research articles are mainly written for experts and often contain terms that are difficult for the general public to understand. Automated lay summarization has become a solution to make biomedical knowledge easier for patients and the public to understand. However, generating lay summaries from full-text articles requires more computing power because the articles are long and costly to process. Fine-tuning large language models for this task also requires substantial resources. This

title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
authors: Yuanjian Xu, Jianing Hao, Tianze Sun et al.
abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsisten

title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
authors: Zhiyuan Wang, Yuezhi Zhou, Ziqi Zhang et al.
abstract: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the \emph{Solution Determin

title: CriticaLLM: Using LLMs as Autonomous Game Master for Tabletop Role-Playing Games
authors: Gaëtan Berlaimont, Justin Vanwichelen, Benoît Ronval et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across many tasks, including processing large amounts of text, following instructions, and generating ideas. This allows the use of such models in various contexts, including games and Tabletop Role-Playing Games (TTRPGs), such as Dungeons & Dragons. However, these games include many complex components, from crafting interesting stories to adhering to rules, while allowing some freedom in players' actions. In this work, we first

title: SCRIBE: Scalable Contextual Representations of Interpretable Brain-Grounded Semantics
authors: Camila Kolling, Omer Moussa, Emin Çelik et al.
abstract: Understanding how the human brain constructs meaning from real-world language remains a fundamental challenge, as semantics depend on context that varies in natural settings. To enable the study of real-world linguistic meaning in the brain, we introduce SCRIBE, a framework grounded in a neuroscience-informed semantic space that leverages an ensemble of open-source large language models to generate interpretable, word-level semantic representations of arbitrary text. In a behavioral study with 9

title: FlashAttention with Statistics: Low-Overhead Attention Features for Compact Hallucination Detectors
authors: Andrei Volodichev, Maksim Savichev, Nikita Sviridov et al.
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. title: Ontology Refinement with Embeddings and LLMs: A Case Study on CASTON
authors: Hui Yang, Ziyu Li, Xuan Liu et al.
abstract: Ontologies are widely used to represent and organize complex knowledge in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare. However, constructing reliable ontologies remains challenging, as class hierarchies, whether manually or automatically constructed, may contain subtle subsumption errors that require careful refinement. We study this problem in CASTON, a casting-domain ontology, and present a lightweight but scalable refinement workflow that combines a fine-tuned ontology embedding model with Lar

title: Translation Circuit Discovery and Targeted Optimization for Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
authors: Atai Waris Khan, Abdullah Mazhar, Raghu Kumar et al.
abstract: Recent multilingual large language models achieve strong translation performance, yet the internal mechanisms responsible for low-resource multilingual translation remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we study translation circuits in multilingual decoder-only LLMs for Hindi-to-Urdu and Hindi-to-Sindhi (Devanagari). We propose TITAN, a mechanistic framework that combines causal intervention, sparse feature decomposition, and targeted preference optimization to identify and optimize cr

title: Identifying Effective Strategies in Prompt Evolution for Stress and Emotion Prediction
authors: SeungHyun Yi, Seungjun Yi, Sriram Sattiraju et al.
abstract: Early stress detection and risk prediction are crucial for timely mental health assessment and support. While large language models have recently shown promise for social media stress prediction, relying on accuracy can obscure false positives. Also, prompt revisions yield inconsistent gains across models and tasks, with unclear links to strategy combinations and instruction changes. By comparing six methods on social media stress and emotion data across two model sizes, we found that GEPA and i

title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
authors: Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli et al.
abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gath

title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
authors: Wenqiu Tang, Zhen Wan, Yihui Wang et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting t

title: VoteGEO-Bench: Measuring the Impact of Generative Engine Optimization on Electoral Visibility
authors: Shiqi Zhang, Xiaokui Xiao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for election information, yet little is known about how external web content shapes the political information they present. Generative engine optimization (GEO) rewrites web content to improve its visibility in generated responses. To investigate its potential risks in voting scenarios (VoteGEO), we introduce VoteGEO-Bench, a benchmark covering the 2024 U.S. presidential election and the 2026 Japanese House of Representatives election, combining

title: LLM-Based Weak Annotation for Cybersecurity Tweet Classification: A Teacher-Student Framework
authors: Ferry Afit Kurniawan, Kazushi Okamoto, Koki Karube et al.
abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) relies on the timely identification of emerging threats, enabling organizations and security analysts to support situational awareness and decision-making. Social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter) have become valuable CTI sources because vulnerabilities and attack activities are often discussed there before appearing in formal reports. However, the rapid growth of cybersecurity discussions on social media has created more content than domain experts can

title: FGSS-BO: Feedback-Guided Hypothesis Management for LLM-Based Bayesian Optimization
authors: Hao Chen, Ziyang Ling, Ronald X. Xu et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. title: KBS: A Korean Benchmark Suite for Foundation Model Evaluation
authors: Yeonkyoung So, Jongmin Kim, Sungmok Jung et al.
abstract: We present a Korean Benchmark Suite (KBS) comprising Ko-ARC, Ko-GSM8K, Ko-EQ-Bench, Ko-WinoGrande, Ko-LAMBADA, and Ko-IFEval, covering six capabilities across 9,396 items. The suite combines review, localization, direct Korean construction, and redesign for Korean, avoiding a translation-only approach to benchmark adaptation. We evaluate Korean-developed models, multilingual open models, and closed API models under protocols that account for model access, prompt format, and scoring differences.

title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
authors: Dongyu Gong
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
authors: Chaogui Gou
abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood.

title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
authors: Swati Gupta, Tianjiao Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream t

title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
authors: Michael Beigl
abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.

title: INCONVENIENT: A Benchmark to Assess LLM Generalization Capabilities from Convenience Samples
authors: Sara Rezaeimanesh, Chad Klochko, Kundan Thind et al.
abstract: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observatio

title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
authors: Maxence Faldor, Satinder Singh, Roberta Raileanu
abstract: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. title: Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions
authors: Ying Fang, Zhifu Gao, Qing Gu et al.
abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision

title: MindEval2: Clinically Grounded Patients and Rubrics for Evaluating Language Models in Mental Health Support
authors: John Mendonça, Daniel Tschernutter, José Pombal et al.
abstract: With people increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, the need to evaluate these tools is becoming more pressing. Recent benchmarks attempt to mimic a realistic setting by simulating multi-turn interactions with synthetic patients and evaluating them with an LLM-as-a-judge. However, the usefulness of these methods is limited because simulated patients can be overly forthcoming and self-reflective, and judgments typically involve opaque Likert scales with unclear practical ut

title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
authors: Ian Gemp, Shubhendu Trivedi, Adam Fisch et al.
abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. title: Augment the Cache, Replace the Activation: A 2x2 Study of Internal-State Sharing
authors: Adam Deng, Shicheng Liu, Yada Zhu
abstract: Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an age

title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
authors: Adam Deng, Shicheng Liu, Yada Zhu
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written

title: From Research Goals to Scientific Closure: Evaluating Agents Through Evidence-Supported Physics Research
authors: Yijia Mao, Song Dai, Tao Chen et al.
abstract: Can AI agents organize scientific investigations that lead to well-supported conclusions? To evaluate this capability, we introduce PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring physics areas. Each task specifies the research objective and essential scientific constraints, while leaving the agent to organize the investigation and determine how to generate and validate the evidence needed to answer the questio

title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
authors: Yukun Tian, Junwei Su, Haofeng Xu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and

title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
authors: Boyu Cui, Junhao Luo, Zhihao Wang et al.
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk pre

title: SITAR: A Situational Distortion Metric for Automatic Speech Recognition Evaluation
authors: Mingzhe Lu, Jinhao Liu, Yunpeng Li et al.
abstract: In automatic speech recognition (ASR), transcription errors with similar lexical or semantic discrepancies can have markedly different consequences for the situation conveyed by speech. Capturing these differences requires not merely contextual assessment, but an understanding of what the spoken discourse describes, establishes, or seeks to bring about. However, relying on LLM judges introduces computational cost and scoring variability. We introduce SITAR, a situational distortion metric for AS

title: Two Sample Sizes in Test-Time LLM Ensembling: Buffered ERM and Minimax Theory
authors: Zhi Zhang, Arash A. Amini
abstract: Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: $Q$ labeled questions and $N$ generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's

title: ZoomCap: Evidence-Routed Visual Zooming for Recoverable Visual Information Transfer
authors: Hao Shi, Jiafeng Wang, Yuzhuo Fu et al.
abstract: Detailed captions transfer visual information into vision-language model supervision, but quality is easily conflated with length: long single-pass outputs still miss small objects, text, and spatial relations or promote uncertain observations into confident claims. We formulate fine-grained captioning as recoverable visual information transfer, in which a teacher acquires missing evidence under a finite observation budget and converts it into reusable supervision. ZoomCap uses a draft caption t

title: Condition-Contrastive Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation of Language Models
authors: Wenxuan Luo, Chenxi Li, Haoyue Liu et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves a student language model by training on its own generated trajectories with supervision from a stronger teacher. However, when conditioned on student-generated prefixes, the teacher can favor invalid continuations that violate the question's premises, causing OPD to encourage erroneous reasoning steps. title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
authors: Fazle Mohammed Tasfiq, Sabab Attin, Sheikh Md. Tahmid Hossain et al.
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms. In the realm of LLM, the last two years have seen tremendous progress in RAG architectures, with many models reporting to have improved performance through various design innovations. title: GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Yining Tang, Junyu Zhang, Haomiao Qiu et al.
abstract: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
authors: Artin Tajdini, Manpreet Kaur, Peng Qi
abstract: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal et al.
abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong et al.
abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise

title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
authors: Delip Rao, Ahmed Muharram, Chris Callison-Burch
abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot

title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
authors: Alicia Colmenero-Fernández
abstract: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. title: From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation
authors: Xiaoxuan Dong, Jin Zhang, Zichen Yuan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face tasks from unseen domains and execution contexts, making zero-shot tool selection essential for identifying tools that can satisfy task requirements. Existing dominant methods mainly rely on relevance ranking, but semantic matching alone cannot ensure that a tool is functionally compatible or remains applicable in a new context. title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
authors: Yuyao Ge, Shenghua Liu, Peizhong Gao et al.
abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. title: CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval
authors: Xinyi Cheng, Tianfu Zhang, Jiwen Li et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate multiple retrieval actions jointly, while downstream systems often provide only one reward for the resulting set. Broadcasting this reward provides a valid score-function gradient estimator for the expected set-level objective, but does not determine a coalition-dependent within-set attribution. We introduce CASI (Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval), which constructs the missing counterfactual information through snapshot-grou

title: EvalBuilder: Can LLMs Build Efficient Benchmarks?
authors: Huaisheng Zhu, Hangfan Zhang, Teng Xiao et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for long-horizon research and engineering, yet evaluating these capabilities remains expensive, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on human expertise. This motivates a natural question: can LLM agents themselves construct efficient benchmarks that preserve the conclusions of costly reference evaluations? title: Explorer-Zero: Improving Self-Play for Long-Horizon Tasks with Decomposable Verifiable Rewards
authors: Tianyu Liu, Davide Belli, Bence Major et al.
abstract: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer

title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
authors: Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu et al.
abstract: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
authors: Huining Yuan, Xiangmin Yi, Zelai Xu et al.
abstract: Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student's behavior with the teacher's. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue

title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
authors: Shiv Muthupandiyan, Tolga H. Dur, Mac Walker et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of informa

title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Seojin Hwang, Youngmin Choi, Hwanhee Lee
abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun et al.
abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Bas

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
authors: Chenhao Yuan, Bohan Yu, Yinhao Xu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Linji Hao, Yanji He, Zihan Wang et al.
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
authors: Yan Xu, Dandan Song, Luan Zhang et al.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
authors: Yilin Jiang, Fei Tan, Xuanyu Yin et al.
abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
authors: Maolin Ran, Minda Chen, Di Huang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
authors: Chihiro Yano, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa et al.
abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable

title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
authors: Alexander Gill, Guram Gogia, Francisco Guzmán
abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
authors: Zhongwei Xie, Xingsu Li, Jingqiao Yu et al.
abstract: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. title: XferAgent: Cross-Agent Experience Transfer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
authors: Weihao Li, Jun Bai, Shijie Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can reuse experience from prior task executions to improve performance on subsequent tasks. Although existing methods enable cross-agent experience sharing, differences in agents' execution histories and task requirements make shared experiences difficult to reuse effectively. title: $τ$-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
authors: Rishitosh Kumar Singh, Amir Saeidi, Shamanthak Hegde et al.
abstract: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi et al.
abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
authors: Ashish Acharya, Aman Al Amin, Hong Qin
abstract: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
authors: Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li et al.
abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. title: MemCode: Discrete Semantic Representations for Long-Term Agent Memory
authors: Xin Li, Liang Hu, Duoqian Miao et al.
abstract: Long-term memory remains a fundamental bottleneck for large language model (LLM) agents across sessions. Existing systems typically adopt a write-then-retrieve paradigm, storing context-dependent dialogue fragments and retrieving them via nearest-neighbor search in a continuous embedding space. This design yields unstable access units and systematically misses logically related but lexically distant evidence. We propose MemCode, a long-term agent memory framework that couples retrieval-oriented

title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents
authors: Qianhong Guo, Wei Xie, Xiaofang Cai et al.
abstract: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
authors: Chenxu Wang, Xiaoyu Wen, Han Qi et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents
authors: Guanhua Zhu, Hanwen Li, Zhi Wei et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Tianle Chen, Pushkar Singh, Ketan Todi et al.
abstract: Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information. We identify this failure as a loop. Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent's history is compressed to fit its context window. title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
authors: Thomas Zeng, Zelei Cheng, Mingyang Zhou et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Minchan Kim, Sungho Bae, Youngjin Kim et al.
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
authors: Sajid Siraj, Maria Barbati
abstract: AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to plan and act over multiple steps, yet models are usually compared per call rather than per completed task. This paper asks: which model should an agent use to complete tasks reliably while minimising energy, cost and time? We show that per-call comparisons can be misleading for agentic AI. title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
authors: Mohsen Iranmanesh, Sina Moradi Sabet, Sina Marefat et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu et al.
abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
authors: Jiatong Li, Yatao Bian
abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech
authors: Ghazal Kalhor, Sima Kamandloo, Mehrsa Shamsian et al.
abstract: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. title: Argument Graph Uncertainty: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Logical Structure of Reasoning Chains
authors: Simon Baur, Sumire Honda, Wojciech Samek et al.
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying large language models in high-stakes reasoning tasks, yet most existing approaches rely on expensive sampling strategies or shallow token-level signals that ignore the internal logical structure of model outputs. title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
authors: Zahraa Al Sahili, Ioannis Patras, Matthew Purver
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei et al.
abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
authors: Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao et al.
abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
authors: Sebastian Nagl
abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu et al.
abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
authors: Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu et al.
abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. title: Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
authors: Mingyeong Kim, Gyusang Cho, Juho Lee et al.
abstract: Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
authors: Yixian Tan, Aulia Adila, Jonathan Heng et al.
abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. title: Learning Perception to Action Rules through Reinforcement Learning for Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
authors: Soyoung Oh, Nursulu Sagimbayeva, Nicholas Jennings et al.
abstract: In Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning, large language models may correctly infer the agent's mental state but fail to use that inference when predicting or judging the agent's subsequent actions. In this work, we investigate whether explicitly connecting perception, belief, and action with rules improves ToM reasoning. title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
authors: Md Rayhanul Masud, S M Maksudul Alam, Mohammad Jaminur Islam
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Xuanyu Meng, Yuji Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specif

title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
authors: Gil Jae Song, Sungjoo Yoo
abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution
authors: Minseok Ko, Hyunseok Lee, Woomin Song et al.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
authors: Kutay Tire, Atula Tejaswi, Haris Vikalo et al.
abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. title: Integrating Simulation and Chain-of-thought Reasoning in Multimodal-Language Models For Physical Reasoning
authors: YingQiao Wang, Eric Bigelow, Tomer Ullman et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models often need to reason about the physical dynamics of the world in order to answer questions appropriately. Various methods have emerged for solving physical reasoning tasks, and in particular, two leading approaches are Chain-of-Thought reasoning and physics-grounded simulation. title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Shuyuan Zheng, Yun-seo Lee, Xing Gao et al.
abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang et al.
abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
authors: Yinzhen Huang, Jiahe Xie, Yitong Sun et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
authors: Taha Sabir, Alberto Montero Molina, Thinh Quang Ly et al.
abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
authors: Oscar Chew, Po-Yi Lu, Yi-Jie Cheng et al.
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. title: Manacá-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge
authors: Bruno Leonardo Santos Menezes, Carlos Leonardo Souza Cardoso, Fabio André Machado Porto
abstract: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
authors: Rusali Saha, Nitya Khurana, Ruihong Huang et al.
abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries.
